item.title: Eagles reportedly won't trade Saquon Barkley
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: At a time when some believe the Eagles are in a soft tank, their subtle effort to secure better round-by-round draft position in 2027 won't include getting an extra draft pick or two for running back Saquon Barkley.
item.content:encoded:
At a time when some believe the Eagles are in a soft tank, their subtle effort to secure better round-by-round draft position in 2027 won't include getting an extra draft pick or two for running back Saquon Barkley.

NFL Network reports that the Eagles won’t trade Barkley before the November 10 deadline.

It's clear, unequivocal. The Eagles aren't playing the "no plans" game, like the Raiders are with Maxx Crosby. The Eagles, based on the report, are moving forward with Barkley.

Of course, the emergence of the report nine days before the deadline could be an indication that the Eagles have realized there's no offer forthcoming that would get them to accept taking a $26 million dead-money charge for Barkley in 2027.

The Eagles have already traded a veteran player, when Cam Jurgens was shipped to the Ravens in the aftermath of Lane Johnson's surprise retirement. That doesn't mean that the Eagles will have a Colts-style fire sale — especially as to any contracts that, if traded, would pour jet fuel on the cap situation next year.

Given the cap consequences, it would make much more sense to trade Barkley after June 1 of 2027. Like they did when trading receiver A.J. Brown after June 1 of 2026.

That move followed months of reports and claims and assertions that they wouldn't be trading Brown. So, yes, it will make plenty of sense to pay attention to any and all chatter that may emerge in the offseason, leading up to a potential June 1 move if the Eagles believe that 2027 could shape up to be another soft-tank season, too.

item.title: The new allegations against Josh Jacobs could create a credibility issue
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Friday's release of police records in the Josh Jacobs case brought to light allegations made by three other women against the Packers running back.
item.content:encoded:
Friday's release of police records in the Josh Jacobs case brought to light allegations made by three other women against the Packers running back.

It also creates a problem for Jacobs, based on the things he may have said to the league.

Although there has been no indication that the league has summoned Jacobs to Manhattan for a formal interview in advance of the potential imposition of discipline (that's often the final step in the investigation), it's possible — if not likely — that the NFL has had conversations with Jacobs before and/or during his six-game stint on paid leave.

One obvious question to ask Jacobs is whether the incident for which he pleaded no contest to misdemeanor battery charges was a one-time thing, or whether it has happened before. If the question was asked, and if Jacobs said there are no other incidents, the emergence of new allegations will impact his credibility in the eyes of the league.

Even if the NFL's effort to explore the new allegations goes nowhere (the league has no subpoena power to compel cooperation by the others who spoke to the authorities in Wisconsin), the mere existence of three additional claims will make the league view anything Jacobs has told them more skeptically.

Regardless of how it plays out, the evidence of the other claims against Jacobs reshuffles the deck, both for the league and for the Packers. The fact that they've been linked to trade talks for Colts running back Jonathan Taylor suggests that the team is already considering whether to move on from Jacobs.

If they do, he could have a hard time finding a landing spot, given the new allegations.

So, yes, it's a real problem for Jacobs. Even though his lawyers have issued a statement downplaying the development, it complicates his standing with the league, with the Packers, and possibly with any other team that could eventually be considering whether to offer him a roster spot, if/when he's no longer a member of the Green Bay organization.

item.title: Colts will take calculated risk, if Jonathan Taylor plays today
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The NFL's injury report places no obligation on teams to disclose that a player will be a healthy scratch.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL's injury report places no obligation on teams to disclose that a player will be a healthy scratch. The world finds out if a player who is able to play otherwise won't be playing roughly 90 minutes before kickoff, when the team supplies its list of inactive players.

For the Colts, there's a decision to be made later this morning. Will running back Jonathan Taylor play at Jacksonville, as they continue to engage in talks aimed at trading him? (The Giants are definitely making a play to get him, and others presumably are, too.)

By all indications, Taylor will play. But if the phone rings before 11:30 a.m. ET and the Colts get an offer they choose not to refuse, the plan could quickly change. (And since the Giants don't have a game this weekend, they can focus their efforts exclusively on trying to get it done, even if it takes a call from coach John Harbaugh to owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon.)

Three weeks ago, the Cardinals knew on Friday that they'd be trading receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. after Sunday's game. Harrison didn't play. It's possible that one of the teams interested in Taylor will put the right terms on the table in order to persuade the Colts to put Taylor in bubble wrap for Sunday pending a post-game announcement that Taylor will be changing teams.

Without a deal in place imminently, the Colts will be taking a calculated risk if Taylor is active. If he gets injured, the trade market will evaporate.

Like it did on Friday for the Commanders and defensive tackle Daron Payne. There were trade talks regarding Payne, until he suffered a season-ending foot injury in practice.

So even though the trade deadline doesn't arrive until November 10, there are various other deadlines that could drive a trade decision. For the Colts, the most immediate deadline arrives very soon, when they have to decide whether to let Taylor play and risk an injury that would necessarily close the door on a potential trade.

item.title: Report: Raiders have "no plans" to trade Maxx Crosby (again)
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Raiders traded defensive end Maxx Crosby in March.
item.content:encoded:
The Raiders traded defensive end Maxx Crosby in March. They won't be trading him in November.

Unless they do.

The official word from Adam Schefter of ESPN is that the Raiders have "no plans" to trade Crosby. We've heard that message plenty of times over the years from teams that had "no intent" or "no intention" or "no plan" to trade a player.

Until they traded him.

It happened this week. The Titans had no plans to trade defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, until they did. They reportedly decided to start listening to the inquiries they were receiving on Tuesday. Two days later, Simmons was in Chicago.

The simple reality is that teams that want Crosby will keep calling the Raiders. If the Raiders lose the next two games before the deadline and fall to 3-6, maybe they'll decide to do what they already decided to do in March.

The trade of Crosby to the Ravens for a pair of first-round picks fell apart after the Ravens decided they weren't comfortable with the condition of his surgically-repaired knee. Still, it shows that the Raiders have already crossed the mental bridge required to pull the pin on a trade. If they did it in March, why wouldn't they do it now — if they get an offer they like?

The problem is that whatever they get now will be compared to what they could have gotten in March. If it's less than two first-round picks, it could be a challenge to sell the move to the fan base.

Or maybe not. After four straight losses, reality has set in for the once 3-0 Raiders. They still have plenty of holes on the roster. Trading Crosby would give them the ability to add young, cheap players. And it would free up cash and cap space to pay other veterans. Even if it's less than two ones, it's more than keeping Crosby through the never-ending rebuild.

In trading Simmons, the Titans added two first-round picks and avoided the bulk of his $105 million extension. The Titans need players, and the Simmons trade will become five or six. The Raiders could do something similar with Crosby, because they need players, too.

For now, they have "no plans." We now wait to see whether, over the next nine days, their plans change.

And what, you say, of the notion that Crosby doesn't want to go? Absent a no-trade clause, he won't have much of a choice. And if/when he lands with a contender, it's hard to imagine that he'd have many complaints.

item.title: Breece Hall is not expected to play against Raiders
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Jets are set to play without running back Breece Hall again this Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
The Jets are set to play without running back Breece Hall again this Sunday.

Hall has missed the last four games with a quad injury and Ian Rapoport of NFL Media reports that he is expected to be inactive against the Raiders. Hall has been practicing on a limited basis for the last two weeks and he's been listed as questionable, but it appears the wait for his return will continue.

Braelon Allen has been the Jets' lead back in Hall's absence. He has 72 carries for 357 yards and a touchdown during his time in the starting lineup.

The Jets are also likely to be without linebacker David Bailey. The first-round pick is listed as doubtful due to a groin injury.

item.title: Thank you for 25 years (get ready for 25 more)
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: From November 1, 2001, to November 1, 2026. And beyond.
item.content:encoded:
It was November 1, 2001. I woke up. I wrote a few blurbs about what was going on in the NFL. I pressed the button. And off we went.

It is November 1, 2026. And here we are.

We wouldn't be here if you weren't reading the stuff we write. It's that simple. Those of you who were around back then had plenty of other options for your time and attention. You've got even more options now. But enough of you have kept coming back (and enough of you have found us in the past 25 years) to keep the lights on, and then some.

After five years of dogpaddling (I quit for a day or so in 2002 because I thought it would never really turn into anything), Sprint came along with a sponsorship deal that made it clear that, sooner or later, PFT would stop being a hobby and start being a full-time job.

I remember not wanting it to become a job, because I didn't want it to ever feel like a job. Even now, it usually doesn't. Even when it does, it's better than every other job I ever had, by a long shot.

None of it happens if you aren't out there, reading the stuff we write, watching PFT Live/#PFTPM or the various clips we attach to the articles, and/or listening to the podcasts. It all changed in 2009 when NBC came along, in every way possible. It's been great for us and, given that NBC keeps extending our contract, presumably good for NBC.

Still, it relies on you. If/when you ever decide you don't care about what we have to say, it's done. I'll keep trying to give you a reason to keep coming back.

For now, we'll keep rolling. It should be a busy day, with some excellent games in the afternoon windows. And the very small token of my appreciation for the folks who have been here the longest — and for everyone else — is the fully re-written Quarterback of the Future. The introduction explains how it came to be the first time around, and its direct connection to getting this operation started in the first place. Basically, without QBF there never would have been PFT.

Chapter One is live. I'll post Chapter Two later today. And one per day, or maybe more often than that, until it's all up. Far more importantly, we'll keep posting the stuff you mainly come here to read, dozens per day and, on some days like today, more than 100.

So thank you. We hope you choose to stick around for the next 25 years, and beyond.

item.title: Ben Johnson: Jeffery Simmons will play a lot, maybe not a full workload Monday night
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: In seven games with the Titans this season, Jeffery Simmons was on the field for 87 percent of defensive snaps and 21 percent of special teams snaps.
item.content:encoded:
In seven games with the Titans this season, Jeffery Simmons was on the field for 87 percent of defensive snaps and 21 percent of special teams snaps. Few defensive tackles in the NFL get that kind of playing time.

And now that he's on the Bears, Simmons probably won't get that kind of playing time on Monday night against the Seahawks. But Bears coach Ben Johnson says Simmons might come close.

Asked if Simmons will play as much on Monday night as he played each week with the Titans, Johnson said it might not be quite that much.

"He might not be quite that high Week 1 for us, but he certainly has shown the ability to carry a load," Johnson said.

Johnson added that he has no doubt Simmons will pick up defensive coordinator Dennis Allen's system quickly.

"He's played a lot of football, he's been in a few different defensive schemes, and I think DA is going to be able to find a spot to do what he does best," Johnson said. "We don't want him thinking out there, and that's what you're conscious of coming into a new team, but he's a smart guy and we've been encouraged by what we've seen so far."

Ultimately, Johnson thinks Simmons will fit in perfectly.

"I just told him I want him to be himself, be his productive self," Johnson said. "He's gonna help us win."

item.title: Josh Allen going for his 102nd win counting playoffs, more than Tom Brady's first 9 seasons
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: If Allen and the Bills win today, he'll surpass Brady for sole possession of the third-most wins in a quarterback's first nine seasons.
item.content:encoded:
By his ninth season in the NFL, Tom Brady had won three Super Bowls and had an undefeated regular season, so it's surprising that any quarterback could win more games than Brady did in his first nine years in the league.

Brady won 101 starts, including both the regular season and the postseason, in his first nine seasons. Bills quarterback Josh Allen also has 101 wins counting the playoffs, so if the Bills beat the Ravens today, Allen will have 102 wins, one more than Brady's total in his first nine seasons.

That's still not the record, however. Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes won 112 games in his first nine seasons, and former Seahawks quarterback Russell Wilson won 107 games in his first nine seasons. So Allen needs to win today and six more times before the Bills' postseason is over to surpass Wilson for second place, and he needs to win today and 11 more times before the Bills' postseason is over to surpass Mahomes for the most wins ever in a quarterback's first nine seasons.

Allen has won 93 regular-season games and eight postseason games in his career. Brady won 87 regular-season games and 14 postseason games in his first nine seasons.

It's worth noting that Brady didn't start at all in his rookie season, and only started one game in his ninth season, suffering a season-ending knee injury in Week 1. Allen started 11 games as a rookie, winning five, and has only missed one game since becoming the Bills' starter.

Allen is racking up an impressive career résumé, even as he still hasn't done is what Brady did more than anyone else in NFL history: Get to, and win, a Super Bowl.

item.title: Bill Belichick and UNC nearly upset No. 1 Miami
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Earlier this month, Bill Belichick and North Carolina got a signature win over previously-unbeaten Pitt.
item.content:encoded:
Earlier this month, Bill Belichick and North Carolina got a signature win over previously-unbeaten Pitt. On Saturday night, Belichick and company nearly pulled off a far bigger victory.

The Tar Heels kept it very close against No. 1 Miami, ultimately losing the game 38-35.

North Carolina recovered two onside kicks in an effort to secure possession with less than two minutes to play, after cutting the margin to three points. The first one was wiped out by an offside penalty. The second was nullified by an illegal block.

UNC led the back-and-forth game in the fourth quarter, 28-24. A pair of touchdowns (the second of which was fueled by a UNC turnover) put Miami up by 10, forcing the Tar Heels to score seven and then to attempt to execute a successful onside kick.

After starting 4-2, North Carolina is now 4-4. In his second season in college football, Belichick has a record of 8-12.

item.title: Joe Burrow is one four-TD, no-INT game away from elite club
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The 2026 Bengals have won two, lost two, and then won two.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 Bengals have won two, lost two, and then won two. In their last two, quarterback Joe Burrow has been stellar.

In both the 31-24 Week 5 win over the Dolphins and the 35-13 Week 6 win over the Ravens, Burrow threw four touchdown passes and no interceptions. If he does that again on Sunday against the Titans, Burrow will expand the membership of an elite club by 50 percent.

Per NBC Sports research, another four-TD, no-pick game from Burrow would make him only the third quarterback in NFL history to do it for three straight games. Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford accomplished it in 2025. Then-Packers quarterback Aaron Rodgers was the first to ever do it, in 2016.

The Bengals have beaten the Titans four of five times, including a victory over Tennessee in the 2021 postseason. A win would vault the Bengals into second place in the AFC North, in front of the loser of the Browns-Steelers game.

Unless they tie. In that case, the Browns and Steelers would each be 5-2-1, and the Bengals (with a win on Sunday) would be 5-2.

item.title: Cowboys have a franchise-record 14 straight games with 20 or more points allowed
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Dallas Cowboys have applied to themselves the nickname of "greatest offense there is."
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys have applied to themselves the nickname of "greatest offense there is." While that may be debatable, the team has produced another trend that can't be denied.

Via NBC Sports research, the Cowboys have allowed 20 or more points in 14 straight games. It's the longest active streak in the league, and it's the longest streak in franchise history.

Although on the surface the Cowboys have drawn a favorable opponent on Sunday in the 2-5 Cardinals. But, in recent years, the Cardinals have been a spur in the Dallas saddle. Arizona is 8-1 against the Cowboys, dating back to 2008. The Cardinals also have won four in a row against Dallas — and four in a row at AT&T Stadium.

In 2025, Arizona's third and final win of the year came in Week 9 at Dallas, when the Cardinals beat the Cowboys, 27-17, on a Monday night.

item.title: With 88 yards on Sunday, Derrick Henry will jump to No. 7 all-time in rushing yards
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Ravens running back Derrick Henry, who turns 33 in early January, continues to get it done at a high level.
item.content:encoded:
Ravens running back Derrick Henry, who turns 33 in early January, continues to get it done at a high level. A solid performance on Sunday at Buffalo will put him ahead of a pair of Hall of Famers on the all-time rushing list.

Henry enters the Week 8 game with 13,597 career rushing yards. With only 66 yards, he'll pass Jerome Bettis for No. 8 on the career list. With 88, Henry will leapfrog LaDainian Tomlinson.

If, along the way, Henry scores a rushing touchdown, he'll join Hall of Famers Marshall Faulk and Marcus Allen as the only players with 40 or more rushing touchdowns with multiple teams.

Faulk did it with the Colts and the Rams. Allen did it with the Raiders and the Chiefs. Henry has previously gotten there with the Titans.

The overriding question for Henry is how high he can go on the career rushing list. The current record holder, Hall of Famer Emmitt Smith, believes Henry can catch and beat Smith's all-time record of 18,355 yards.

Henry needs 4,758 yards to match Smith. To get there, Henry probably will have to finish 2026 strong and keep it going for four more years.

By then, it's possible that Henry will be playing for a third team. It would be fitting if the Cowboys — who weren't interested when Henry became a free agent — would be the team with which Henry breaks Smith's record.

item.title: As Eagles prepare for Sunday night, questions of effort from Monday night linger
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: As the Eagles plunged to their fifth straight loss, questions emerged regarding effort, or lack thereof.
item.content:encoded:
As the Eagles plunged to their fifth straight loss, questions emerged regarding effort, or lack thereof.

Or, more fundamentally, whether the defensive line was even bothering to get into their stances.

To no surprise, then, effort was a theme of the week, specifically when reporters had a midweek chance to pose questions to coach Nick Sirianni.

Asked whether there was an issue with effort on Monday night against the Cowboys, and how the coaching staff gauges whether effort is an issue, Sirianni said this: "We grade every play based off of what they did, we grade every play based off of their assignment alignment and we grade every play off of effort. That's not only in games, but that's also at every practice, because if we were just grading it in games and not emphasizing it on every play in every practice, then we wouldn't be doing our job.

"I did not see an effort issue on Monday night. Obviously, it was other things, which I'm sure you guys will ask me about. There were other things, but effort in no way, shape [or] form was an issue there.

"The plays -- now, do you bat 100% on effort? No, you don't play a perfect football game. The plays, anytime there is an effort stand out in a positive way, we show it to the team and show what the standard is. Anytime there's one that we feel like there was a loaf, we point that out and show that to the team. But I didn't think that we had -- I didn't look at the tape and say, 'Hey, this was an effort issue, and this is why this play happened or that play happened.' That's how I graded the film."

He later was asked whether players get grades on a weekly basis regarding topics like assignment, alignment, and effort.

"That would be crazy not to tell them what they've done and what they haven't done," Sirianni said. "We go over that with them. We watch the game with them, and everything is discussed with these guys. I guess I'm a little confused by the question. If we want them to get better, we've got to go over all the mistakes and everything with it."

The reporters eventually attempted to address the confusion by explaining to Sirianni the perception that effort was an issue. So what does Sirianni think about the questions in that regard?

"I think in that situation, everyone's going to look to find answers in a five-game losing streak," Sirianni said. "Just because the result -- If we win that game, do they still question the effort? I don't know. I can't -- I'm not them. My job is to look at the daily process of it and the daily work and what objectively happened in that game and not react based off of the outcome. I get it. I would understand [that] everyone's looking for answers. I don't give you a lot of answers up here. I get that. I understand that. I do respect the job that you guys have to do, but I'm always going to probably keep it tight to the vest.

"But again, it's not about the outcome. . . . We're outcome-aware -- but it is about the process that goes [into] it, what happens Monday through Saturday. What happens Monday through Saturday is usually what happens in the game in my experience. That's why you need great week of preparation, but I'm not letting the outcome dictate how I grade the film. I'm grading the film objectively based off of what I see on a weekly basis."

What everyone sees is a team in a tailspin, with the most recent Super Bowl win fading deep into the rear-view mirror. They get their next chance to turn things around on Sunday night, when they face the 1-4-1 Commanders.

item.title: Jets put DT T'Vondre Sweat on IR
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Jets ruled defensive tackle T'Vondre Sweat out for Week 8 on Friday and they ruled him out for at least three more games on Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
The Jets ruled defensive tackle T'Vondre Sweat out for Week 8 on Friday and they ruled him out for at least three more games on Saturday.

Sweat has been placed on injured reserve due to the knee injury he suffered in last Sunday's loss to the Dolphins. He had 17 tackles and two tackles for loss while starting six of the team's first seven games.

The Jets filled his roster spot by signing defensive tackle Payton Page off of their practice squad. He appeared in four games for the Jets last season.

The Jets also announced that they have elevated offensive lineman Brian Banks and linebacker Quinton Bell from the practice squad. Bell's elevation indicates David Bailey will be inactive after being listed as doubtful with a groin injury.

item.title: Seahawks RBs Zach Charbonnet, Jadarian Price will return Monday night
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The Seahawks will have veteran running back Zach Charbonnet and rookie running back Jadarian Price in the same game for the first time on Monday.
item.content:encoded:
The Seahawks will have veteran running back Zach Charbonnet and rookie running back Jadarian Price in the same game for the first time on Monday.

Neither Charbonnet nor Price has an injury designation for the game against the Bears.

Charbonnet is returning from a torn ACL in his left knee that ended his season on his fifth carry in the divisional round of the 2025 playoffs. He underwent surgery on Feb. 20.

The Seahawks opened his 21-day return-to-practice window on Oct. 1.

Charbonnet ran for 730 yards and 12 touchdowns on 184 carries in the 2025 regular season, while sharing carries with Kenneth Walker.

Price missed the past four games on injured reserve with a chest injury. He has 32 touches for 140 yards.

The Seahawks will have to make a move for Price to return to the active roster from IR.

The team ruled out offensive tackle Charles Cross (ankle), running back Velus Jones (hamstring) and wide receiver Rashid Shaheed (knee). Linebacker Uchenna Nwosu (ankle) is doubtful.

Linebacker Patrick O'Connell (toe), defensive tackle Brandon Pili (back) and quarterback Drew Lock (right elbow) are questionable.

Lock was limited in all three practices this week.

item.title: Deion Sanders and Colorado survive in overtime for first Big 12 win of the season
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: It was harder than it should have been, but Colorado and coach Deion Sanders finally have their first Big 12 win of the season, beating Kansas State 27-24 in overtime to snap a five-game losing streak.
item.content:encoded:
It was harder than it should have been, but Colorado and coach Deion Sanders finally have their first Big 12 win of the season, beating Kansas State 27-24 in overtime to snap a five-game losing streak.

Colorado led for most of the game, and had a 21-14 lead and the ball late in the fourth quarter, but couldn't gain the game-clinching first down, punted, and then nearly choked the game away when Kansas State marched down the field and scored with two seconds remaining in the fourth quarter. With the score 21-20, Kansas State initially lined up to go for two and the win, but then decided to kick the extra point and force overtime.

Kansas State scored a field goal on the opening possession and Colorado responded with a touchdown to win it.

"Our kids, they've never stopped believing," Sanders said after the game. "I'm just so darn proud of these young men right now."

Colorado hasn't given Sanders a lot to be proud of this season, and is now in a last-place tie with Kansas State at 1-4 in the conference. But in what has been a very rough season, Coach Prime finally has a conference win.

item.title: New appeals court ruling could end Sunday Ticket
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: NFL will eventually need to come up with a new way to provide out-of-market games.
item.content:encoded:
Yes, the NFL could "deconstruct" Sunday Ticket in the next wave of broadcast deals. The smart move could be to kill it immediately.

One of the strangest aspects of the NFL's reaction to the $4.7 billion verdict in the class action attacking the pricing of Sunday Ticket was the league's decision to continue to proceed with the same approach to the out-of-market package. The trial judge's decision to throw out the 12-figure verdict (which would have become a 13-figure judgment) seemed to embolden the NFL in this regard, but the decision to wipe out the damages award did not erase the jury's finding that the NFL had violated the antitrust laws.

The argument against Sunday Ticket was fairly simple. The league historically required its Sunday Ticket partner to impose a charge that was high enough to prompt many consumers who would have wanted to watch out-of-market games to settle for the in-market options provided by CBS and Fox.

The lengthy trial transcript (which we obtained and read not long after the verdict was entered) is replete with evidence of the NFL walking a tightrope between maximizing the value of the CBS/Fox packages and the Sunday Ticket offering. Multiple witnesses confirmed that CBS and Fox had open contempt for the Sunday Ticket package, and that the pricing was specifically designed to mollify the networks that were paying enormous fees for the ability to broadcast games in any given market.

But the Sunday Ticket package endures, with ongoing exposure to fresh claims covering the period of time not encompassed by the pending class action. The violation, frankly, continues for each and every Sunday of the football season.

It's somewhat surprising that the NFL has yet to be enjoined from continuing with the lingering antitrust violation. The only recourse is for additional plaintiffs in additional class actions to seek reimbursement for the exorbitant prices they have been charged in order to protect the NFL's relationship with CBS and Fox.

It seems inevitable that the NFL will pull the plug on the Sunday Ticket package, either as a result of a court order or to stop the financial bleeding. The current deal with YouTube runs through 2029. Come 2030 (if not sooner), Sunday Ticket could be replaced with another method of making out-of-market games available to consumers.

The new approach will definitely be cheaper. It possibly could result in the out-of-market Sunday afternoon games being available on a variety of cable channels and/or streamers, with the in-market games still carried by CBS and Fox.

Thus, while today's development in federal appeals court represents very bad news for the league, the end result could be very good news for consumers.

item.title: Appeals court reverses rejection of damages award against NFL in Sunday Ticket class action
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: NFL undoubtedly will appeal the ruling to the U.S. Supreme Court.
item.content:encoded:
This is the kind of Friday afternoon bad news dump that counts as horrible news for the NFL.

Via Mike Scarcella of Reuters, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit has reinstated the $4.7 billion verdict in the Sunday Ticket class action.

The Reuters article, however, apparently has misread the decision. Mark Maske of Front Office Sports characterizes the outcome as ordering a new trial on damages.

"The jury clearly awarded damages based on its improper consideration of the evidence rather than according to the district court’s instructions," the Ninth Circuit wrote, per Maske. "This warrants a new trial on damages. We remand this case for the district court to reinstate the jury’s liability verdict and hold a new damages trial.”

A new trial on damages could result in a lower (or similar or, in theory, higher) final verdict.

The original award, given by a jury in July 2024, was scrapped by the presiding judge over concerns regarding the evidence the plaintiffs presented of economic harm. The judge did not throw out the finding that the NFL had violated federal antitrust laws in the pricing of the Sunday Ticket package.

If/when any verdict becomes an official judgment, the damages will be tripled.

The original verdict sent shock waves through the league, since it ultimately would require each team to come up with $440 million in cash. Statutory interest will push that number even higher.

The NFL undoubtedly will appeal the final decision to the U.S. Supreme Court, which would first have to decide whether to accept the case before issuing a decision. The case possibly would not be ripe for an appeal to the Supreme Court until a new trial on damages happens — if that's what the Ninth Circuit has indeed ordered.

Whatever happens next, the situation instantly becomes the most consequential piece of litigation in the 100-plus-year history of the league.

item.title: After Josh Jacobs was arrested, three other women told police he had abused them, too
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Police records released late on Friday show three women contacted police after Jacobs' May arrest to report similar incidents.
item.content:encoded:
While police were investigating Josh Jacobs following a domestic violence accusation in May, multiple other women reported similar incidents of Jacobs abusing them.

NBC 26 in Green Bay received previously unreleased files in connection with the Jacobs case from the Hobart-Lawrence Police Department late Friday, and those files showed that officers heard from at least three other women who said they had been victims of violence at the hands of Jacobs.

One woman contacted police in June after hearing of Jacobs' May arrest, saying she had been the victim of a similar incident with Jacobs years earlier and was reporting it to police for the first time because she wanted people to believe the woman accusing him in May. That woman said that in January of 2022, Jacobs slapped her across the face, grabbed her by the hair, threw her onto a bed, pinned her down, threw her onto the floor, spit on her and grabbed her by the throat. She also said Jacobs took her phone as she attempted to leave his home.

Another woman also contacted police later in June and said that in April of 2021, Jacobs grabbed her by the arms, pushed her against a wall near a window and threw her belongings outside the home. She said she suffered bruising to her arms and pain and swelling in her rib area. She said she had reported it to the police in a different municipality, and the records released by Hobart-Lawrence Police to NBC 26 indicate that they confirmed with another police department that it did receive that report, but Jacobs apparently was not arrested because the woman had no visible signs of injury.

A third woman told Hobart/Lawrence Police in July that in May of 2022, Jacobs placed his hands on her head and neck, dragged her, scratched her chest, and took her phone. She said she suffered bruising to her arm and scratches to her chest. She said she did not report the incident to police or seek medical attention because Jacobs had told her she could be deported if she had any contact with the authorities.

Jacobs eventually pleaded no contest to misdemeanor battery and criminal damage to property in connection with the May arrest. The NFL placed him on paid leave for the first six games of the season, then allowed him to play starting in Week 7. Jacobs remains subject to a potential NFL suspension for violating the league's personal conduct policy, and the accusations brought by the three other women could be considered by the NFL in determining league discipline.

item.title: Josh Jacobs could be on thin ice in Green Bay
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Throughout his off-field incident that resulted in a no-contest plea to misdemeanor battery, the Packers have remained steadfast in their support of running back Josh Jacobs.
item.content:encoded:
Throughout his off-field incident that resulted in a no-contest plea to misdemeanor battery, the Packers have remained steadfast in their support of running back Josh Jacobs.

That could now be changing.

The persistent presence of the Packers as one of the teams that have expressed some degree of interest in trading for Colts running back Jonathan Taylor suggests that they've at least pondered the possibility of swapping out Jacobs for Taylor.

Recent developments don't help Jacobs's cause.

Beyond the handcuff celebration that Jacobs tried to say wasn’t a handcuff celebration (but that video of the full celebration suggests was a handcuff celebration), Friday's release of police records indicating that at least three other women have accused Jacobs of domestic violence could shake the team's apparent resolve to keep him.

Throw in the fact that Jacobs is averaging 2.3 yards per carry in his two games back from a six-game stint on paid leave — including 1.9 yards per carry against the worst run defense in the league entering Thursday night's game — and it's possible that the Packers will realize that Jacobs is no longer good enough to justify a stubborn circling of the wagons.

Cutting Jacobs would raise the issue of termination pay as to the balance of his $10.2 million salary, and it would short-circuit the team's ability to seek partial repayment of signing-bonus money if/when (when) he's eventually suspended under the Personal Conduct Policy. For now, we won't delve into the full extent of the niceties of Article 30 of the CBA; at a minimum, the Packers would have some potential arguments aimed at cutting off his right to any termination pay.

Even if the Packers ultimately are on the hook for termination pay, it's a sunk cost. The question is whether they want to keep him on the team, in light of recent developments.

Again, they've been linked in multiple reports from ESPNFL to a trade for Jonathan Taylor. That alone is substantial evidence that they're considering a future without Jacobs that could begin sooner rather than later.

item.title: NFL "will review" the new allegations against Josh Jacobs
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Jacobs could be facing a lengthy suspension.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL was already reviewing the case of Packers running back Josh Jacobs following a no-contest plea to misdemeanor battery arising from an incident that happened in May 2026. The league is now investigating additional allegations that have recently come to light.

"We will review these allegations as part of the investigation which has remained open," the NFL said Saturday in a statement.

Police records released on Friday revealed that three other women made allegations of violence against Jacobs, after the first incident came to light. The league likely will need to identify the individuals and then attempt to persuade them to cooperate.

It significantly raises the potential discipline that may eventually be imposed on Jacobs. He'll get credit for the six games he missed on paid leave, with a requirement to forfeit the salary he received.

With the Personal Conduct Policy creating a baseline suspension of six games without pay for each incident of domestic violence, along with enhanced penalties for repeat offenses, Jacobs could be facing a lengthy suspension.

More immediately, the question remains whether the Packers will move on from Jacobs. The team had no comment on Saturday morning, in response to the news that three other women have made allegations against Jacobs.

Through it all, the video of the May 2026 incident remains hidden from public view. The NFL wants to see it before finalizing his punishment for the incident that sparked a no-contest plea.

item.title: Jonathan Taylor trade talks are "active and ongoing"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Seahawks, Packers, Broncos, Vikings, Giants are pegged as potential destinations.
item.content:encoded:
There are two ways to handle the trade of a cornerstone player. One, talk quietly to a minimal number of teams. Like the Titans did with defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. Two, throw the doors open and try to get the best possible package of draft picks and/or players in return. Like the Colts are now doing with running back Jonathan Taylor.

Indianapolis has officially declared that Taylor is available, via a selective and strategic leak to ESPNFL. Trade talks are "active and ongoing," per the report.

The teams that have "expressed at least some level of interest" are the Broncos, Packers, Vikings, Giants, and Seahawks.

Last weekend's Sunday Splash! report that operated as the "everything must go" sign for the Colts pegged the Broncos, Packers, Vikings, and Seahawks as potentially interested teams in Taylor. The Giants (who are believed, we're told by multiple sources, to have been pursuing Simmons) are a new arrival. Which would possibly be bad news for second-year running back Cam Skattebo, who emerged from the doghouse last week with 124 rushing yards. (It wouldn't be a surprise if the Giants offered Skattebo to the Colts as part of the trade package, frankly.)

To the extent that tying four teams to the trade talks doesn't get the Colts maximum compensation, the new report notes that the Colts "would prefer" that Taylor stick around for their "rebuild."

If they really wanted Taylor, they wouldn't be fielding trade offers fo him.

The Colts reportedly are looking for a package similar to what the 49ers sent to the Panthers in 2022 for running back Christian McCaffrey: a second-round pick, a third-round pick, and a fourth-round pick in the 2023 draft and a fifth-round pick in the 2024 draft.

The next question is whether Taylor will play on Sunday. It's possible, in our view, the Colts will hold Taylor out of action on Sunday at Jacksonville, like the Cardinals did three weeks ago when they had a deal in place to trade receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. to the Texans. Even without a deal, keeping Taylor out of the game would ensure that he won't get injured.

If that happens, rookie Seth McGowan would be the likely starter in Week 8. Last Sunday, the seventh-rounder who played for Kentucky last year had 11 carries for 48 yards in a 16-10 loss to the Vikings.

And the Vikings continue to make the most sense for Taylor. Especially since they had the best possible opportunity to scout him six days ago, when he had 18 carries for 95 yards and an Adrian Peterson-style 38-yard touchdown run.

If the Vikings add Taylor in the coming days, he'd likely make his debut as soon as next Monday night, when the Vikings host the Bills. And when they put Peterson in the team's Ring of Honor.

item.title: Report: John Harbaugh called Amy Adams Strunk directly in an effort to land Jeffery Simmons
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Harbaugh's unconventional move failed to prevent Bears from doing deal with Titans.
item.content:encoded:
The trade that sent defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons from the Titans to the Bears has an interesting — and unusual — postscript.

Jonathan Jones of The Athletic reports that Giants coach John Harbaugh directly called Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk in an effort to get Simmons to New York.

The call reportedly came after Giants G.M. Joe Schoen had contacted Titans G.M. Mike Borgonzi about Simmons, only to be told that the Titans weren't trading him.

As Jones notes, another G.M. who learned about the effort said it "violates a code" among football's decision-makers. One source in a key football position with one of the NFL's teams dubbed the effort "shameful."

Despite Borgonzi's claim from Thursday that the Titans weren't looking to trade Simmons until the Bears called on Wednesday night, Jones reports that the Titans' "braintrust" had a meeting on Tuesday during which they decided to start listening to offers for Simmons.

It's unclear whether Harbaugh made the call to Adams before or after Bears G.M. Ryan Poles offered a package that included a pair of first-round picks. We're told the Giants were willing to offer more than what the Bears ultimately sent to the Titans. (Of course, that's easy to say at this point.)

The entire situation underscores the value of pre-existing relationships when it comes to getting deals done. It was a point we discussed on Friday's PFT Live. In 2021, the trade that sent quarterback Matthew Stafford from the Lions to the Rams had a distinct "inside job" feel to it, given that Lions G.M. Brad Holmes had recently been hired from the Rams.

Other teams that would have been interested in attempting to acquire Stafford were surprised to learn that he had been quietly and quickly dealt to the Rams, who were able to tuck quarterback Jared Goff into the deal — and to discreetly attach extra compensation to get the Lions to take on a contract that, after only two seasons, the Rams had come to regret. The outcome prompted former Commanders G.M. Martin Mayhew to call every team in the league the following offseason to inquire as to whether their starting quarterback may be available in trade.

The ultimate question, when trades like this happen, is whether the relationship angle results in the team that gives up a key player getting as much as it could. If the Giants would have indeed offered more, shouldn't the Titans have fully explored that avenue? Ultimately, the longstanding relationship between Poles and Borgonzi may have superseded the effort to get as much as possible for Simmons.

item.title: NFL fines Caleb Williams $23,882 for "unauthorized logo" on shoes in Week 7
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: NFL doubles the fine amount from Week 6; Williams has said he won't back down.
item.content:encoded:
As to Caleb Williams, the NFL currently stands for the 'Nother Fine League.

Per a source with knowledge of the situation, the NFL has fined the Bears quarterback $23,882 for wearing an "unauthorized logo" on his shoes during the Week 7 game against the Patriots. That represents double the amount of the $11,941 fine imposed on Williams last week for wearing the forbidden footwear in Week 6 against the Falcons.

Williams has said that he plans to continue wearing Caddix shoes, which do not have a deal with the league. He presumably will appeal the second fine.

“I’m huge into trying to stay on the field," Williams said Wednesday. "I’m huge into trying to be healthy. It’s a rough game and things like that. So the cleats, they’ve been great. They’ve been super comfy and they’ve worked. They are a science-type of cleat. It’s something that focuses on when you plant on the hard plants on turf or grass, they call them SmartStuds, and they move when you move in these hard plants. They take tension off of your tendons, your joints and all of that. So over the course of a long career or over the course of a long year, when you can take some percentage -- it could be one, it could be 50, it could be 12, it could be whatever, you know. When you take that percentage off consistently over a period of time, you know, you get to have the chance, a higher chance of being healthy. And so that’s what I focus on.

“I try to be healthy. They’re smart cleats. They’re science cleats, and they’ve been working for me. A bunch of other guys wear them in the league, and they’re forward-focused on making sure players stay on the field, and that’s what I’m always focused on."

The appeal of Williams's fine for Week 6 has not yet been resolved.

Presumably, the league will continue to impose fines in increasing amounts unless and until Williams complies. At some point, the league could (in theory) prevent Williams from playing in the non-conforming shoes. Neither fine letter, however, warns him that he could be kept from playing with the Caddix shoes.

item.title: Report: NFL flexes referee Alex Moore's crew out of prime time
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The NFL, for reasons still neither known nor apparent, opted not to flex the game between the 2-5 Eagles and 1-4-1 Commanders out of prime time, despite multiple other compelling Sunday afternoon games.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL, for reasons still neither known nor apparent, opted not to flex the game between the 2-5 Eagles and 1-4-1 Commanders out of prime time, despite multiple other compelling Sunday afternoon games.

The league did, however, flex the officiating crew out of the Sunday night game.

Via Football Zebras, Alex Moore's crew has been moved from Eagles-Commanders to Patriots-Dolphins. Shawn Hochuli's crew will work the Sunday night game.

The report, citing unnamed officiating sources, says that the change is "more about optics rather than a disciplinary action."

Whatever the precise reason, it seems to be a reaction to the various bad calls Moore's crew made in the Week 7 game between the Packers and Lions, including two questionable roughing the passer calls on the Packers and a phantom illegal hit on a defenseless player by Lions linebacker Derrick Barnes.

The optics-driven reason is simple. Moving Moore's crew out of prime time, and relegating them to a secondary 4:25 p.m. ET broadcast on CBS, avoids Mike Tirico and/or Cris Collinsworth mentioning the rough day the crew had in Detroit.

Typically, the various crews are assigned without regard to the broadcast footprint of a given game. In this specific case, it shows that the league would rather avoid further talk about the multiple mistakes that Moore's crew made.

Even though Raiders minority owner Tom Brady did an effective job of highlighting those mistakes to an audience of 24.67 million on Sunday.

item.title: Of eight use of helmet infractions in Week 7, only Cam Skattebo was flagged
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The fine imposed on Giants running back Cam Skattebo for illegal use of the helmet was not a rarity.
item.content:encoded:
The fine imposed on Giants running back Cam Skattebo for illegal use of the helmet was not a rarity. The flag thrown in real time for it was.

Of eight fines levied by the NFL for use-of-helmet violations in Week 7, only Skattebo's came with a flag.

The league fined Skattebo $7,073. The seven players fined but not flagged were: Bears cornerback Clark Phillips ($11,550); Broncos safety Brandon Jones ($23,882); Broncos Alex Singleton ($47,662); Lions safety Brian Branch ($23,882); Colts cornerback Cam Taylor-Britt ($7,791); Steelers receiver Brandon Smith ($4,916); and 49ers running back Jordan James ($6,194).

The fines increase as the violations repeat. For Singleton, who was fined $23,882 for illegal use of the helmet, it was the second straight week he was fined.

The officials, for whatever reason, don't often call penalties for illegal use of the helmet. That's what made the penalty called on Skattebo so unusual.

The fact that the hit flattened Texans safety M.J. Stewart likely was a factor in the decision to penalize Skattebo. Still, the fact that only one of eight instances resulted in a foul being called underscores the fact that, when it comes to the rule against lowering the helmet and initiating forcible contact against an opponent, it's something that costs players money far more routinely than it costs their teams field position.

item.title: Chargers place DB Derwin James on IR
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: Chargers defensive back Derwin James hasn't played since Sept. 27.
item.content:encoded:
Chargers defensive back Derwin James hasn't played since Sept. 27. He won't play again until at least Nov. 29.

The Chargers announced they placed James on injured reserve on Saturday.

James has missed four games with a hamstring injury, and coach Jim Harbaugh revealed earlier this week that the five-time Pro Bowler had a setback in his rehab.

He has 21 tackles and a pass defensed in three games.

In a corresponding move, the Chargers signed cornerback Isas Waxter to the active roster from the practice squad. They also elevated cornerback Kaiir Elam from the practice squad for Sunday's game.

Waxter has two tackles this season, playing 17 defensive snaps and 19 on special teams in two games.

Elam has not played this season but has 43 appearances in his five seasons.

item.title: Dolphins elevate Zane Gonzalez, Max Llewellyn
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The Dolphins elevated kicker Zane Gonzalez and edge rusher Max Llewellyn to the active roster for Sunday’s game, the team announced.
item.content:encoded:
The Dolphins elevated kicker Zane Gonzalez and edge rusher Max Llewellyn to the active roster for Sunday’s game, the team announced.

Gonzalez, 31, signed with the Dolphins' practice squad on Oct. 20 and kicked in last week's win over the Jets. He made all four extra points.

He replaced Riley Patterson, whom the team released.

Gonzalez was previously with the Dolphins during the offseason program and training camp. He was placed on injured reserve in August and released with an injury settlement on Aug. 19.

In nine games for Atlanta last season, Gonzalez hit 19-of-22 field goals and 17-of-18 extra points.

Llewellyn has appeared in two games for the Dolphins this season, making his NFL debut in Week 2 against the 49ers and appearing in Sunday's victory over the Jets.

He was selected by the Dolphins in the seventh round after a five-year career at Iowa.

item.title: Broncos will put running back R.J. Harvey on injured reserve after injury in practice
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Broncos running back R.J.
item.content:encoded:
Broncos running back R.J. Harvey will miss at least the next four games.

Harvey is going on injured reserve because of a knee injury he suffered in practice this week, according to Ian Rapoport.

An injured reserve stint has to last at least four games, so Harvey will be on IR for at least tomorrow against the Chiefs, Week 9 against the Panthers, the Week 10 bye, Week 11 against the Raiders and Week 12 against the Steelers. He will be eligible to return in Week 13, December 6 against the Dolphins.

Harvey is a backup who plays a lot on third downs and is the Broncos' top receiver out of the backfield, with 25 catches for 217 yards this season. He also has 24 carries for 87 yards.
